title: Poggle and the Polishing Lizard
markdown:
The land wore fog like a secret it enjoyed. Hills tickled the sky. Mountains stood like giants who had agreed to nap standing up. Slate roofs shone after rain, fish-scale bright. Paths vanished into grey as if the mist were playing a game with destinations.

Poggle the goblin had ideas that arrived like sun on a stream: inventions, clever joins, a better way to hold a screw. When the custom asked him to choose a familiar—a creature to walk beside him for good—the ideas tangled, yarn in a breeze. Mottle, his lizard, emerald and sapphire, blinked old wise eyes and said nothing, which was their oldest conversation. Not a pet. A pulse.

“It is today,” Poggle whispered. Mottle’s tail ticked once.

The Mountain Market could spin a head. Fog thinned just enough to show banners, then thickened to hide the prices. Sellers called in a dozen keys. A Sock-Finding Squirrel, guaranteed against sofa cushions and the particular malice of washing lines. A Gloom-Busting Gnat in a jar, hum guaranteed cheerful, slightly accusing if you stayed sad on purpose. A Slow-Motion Snail Melody Player, music so slow it was nearly still, recommended for people who found ordinary time too hasty. Poggle’s eyes collected them the way he collected screws: thoroughly, and then he did not know which one belonged. None sat right. They were good, loud, and the wrong shape for his quiet. Mottle tasted the air and declined to audition.

Then Mayor Grumbletoe arrived, belly first, voice like happy thunder that had not asked. A banner the size of a modest weather: THE GREAT GARGOYLE HOIST. ALL GARGOYLES MUST SIT ON THE TOWN-SQUARE ROOFTOPS. FOR SAFETY AND SUPER DUPER BEAUTY. Gold letters. Friendly arrows. Drawings of stone beasts looking unconvincingly pleased.

A murmur. Gargoyles were grumpy by profession. Moving them meant cracked tiles and offended guardians. The signs, however, were a masterpiece of persuasion. Poggle frowned. A terrible idea, packaged as a festival. More distracting than any snail.

“Come, Mottle. Ignis Scribe.”

The climb to Ignis took the rest of the morning and a polite argument with a path that kept dissolving. Poggle talked to Mottle about levers, then about signs, then about nothing, which Mottle preferred. The dragon librarian lived in a cavern on the highest misted peak, shelves of scrolls and fat leather going farther than courtesy, ladders that assumed you had wings. She hated dust. One puff, one speck, and her sigh could rearrange a mountain’s opinion. A notice by the entrance asked visitors to wipe their ideas as well as their feet.

They found her wiping a star map that had tried to gather a century. Scales the colour of old paper. Eyes warm gold, tired and faintly amused. A kettle somewhere smelled of smoke that had been trained. Mottle had already claimed a patch of sun that had no business being indoors.

“Poggle. And your companion. Still choosing?”

“The market is a bewilderment. Grumbletoe wants to move gargoyles. The signs are… excellent.”

A soft puff; a grain of ash. “His signs are good. His ideas are pink libraries. He asked me once to paint this place for happier scholars. Imagine the dust.”

Poggle felt ordinary beside her size and the Mayor’s gold. Just a goblin and a lizard who followed.

Ignis tapped a fancy cover. “The best familiars are not under banners. Shared looks. Loyalty that does not need a stall. Not the loudest roar. The truest quiet.”

Poggle’s gaze found Mottle instead of the fancy cover. Mottle, who knew when Poggle’s hands shook over a decision and came to sit on the nearest blueprint. Who sat through hours of tinkering while the fog pressed the windows. Who had once nudged a dropped screw back into his palm without theatre, a silent correction more useful than a market’s guarantees. Warmth on a bad-dream cheek, scales like a small stove. The sock squirrel would never have done that. Certainty arrived without a speech, a bloom warmer than the cavern sun-patch.

“I think I have found him.”

In the square Grumbletoe swept an arm at his arrows. “Safer. More beautiful. More impressive.”

Poggle stepped forward. Mottle sat on his shoulder like a small living crown. The crowd turned, surprised to find the banner had competition.

“Your signs organise beautifully,” Poggle said, voice carrying because it had somewhere to stand. “They miss a detail. Gargoyles are stone. Heavy. Not cheerful. And some familiars are better at certain jobs.”

He set Mottle on the Mayor’s important cloth. An elegant tail found a loose corner. The snout polished an almost invisible smudge from a gold letter. The gold, insulted into shining, shone.

“Mottle polishes. He keeps signs—and stone—spotless. One speck, and he hisses. Loudly. And if he were to nudge a gargoyle that sat a little wobbly, or looked too grumpy, and it slipped… especially onto a really important sign underneath… that would be unfortunate.”

The crowd gasped on cue. Grumbletoe stared. Mottle flicked a tongue, innocent as dust. The Mayor pictured frantic sign-painters, tumbling guardians, and a lizard’s judging gaze. The hoist shrank.

“Perhaps we rethink. Safety. Extra sparkle.”

Cheers, the useful kind, the sort that does not require a second banner. Someone slapped Poggle’s back and then apologised to Mottle. Grumbletoe rolled the hoist plan into a tube that looked less golden from the end. Poggle’s grin was relief more than triumph. He walked home through fog that had decided to be kind, lizard warm against his neck. He had not needed a roar, or a squirrel, or a gnat with a tune. He had needed the familiar who had been on his shoulder the whole walk to the market, polishing the day without being asked, and hissing only at genuine specks.
characters: Poggle (goblin Poggle), Mottle (lizard Mottle), Ignis Scribe (a dragon librarian who dislikes soot on the books)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
